hero.headline: St. Lucie County Fire District says 3 fired, 2 suspended after hazing investigation
hero.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District says it terminated three employees and suspended two others following an independent investigation into allegations that senior personnel used a
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District says it terminated three employees and suspended two others following an independent investigation into allegations that senior personnel used a modified bug zapper to electrically shock junior firefighters while they were on duty.

The district released a statement Saturday, July 18, along with a 2025 workplace culture analysis and a May 2026 investigative report detailing the incidents.

According to the documents, firefighter-paramedic Roberto "Rocky" Tapia provided videos and photographs to district administrators in March 2026. Investigators determined that several of the recordings showed incidents that occurred at Station 1 in March and September 2024.

The device was reportedly constructed from a dismantled bug zapper and modified so it could deliver electrical shocks to people.

One video showed then-probationary employee and paramedic apprentice Matthew Lohse seated in a chair while senior employees asked him paramedic-related questions. Investigators said Lohse was shocked when he answered incorrectly as other employees watched and laughed.

Other videos showed then-probationary or apprentice firefighters Kyle Kirkham and John Edmondson being shocked multiple times. The report noted that the employees appeared to experience pain, including yelling, groaning, twitching and pulling away from the device.

Several witnesses told the investigator that the junior employees had consented to participating. Lohse, Kirkham and Edmondson also said they had agreed to be shocked.

However, independent investigator John "J.K." Keller concluded that the power imbalance between senior personnel and probationary employees undermined the credibility of those claims of consent.

The investigation found that only junior, probationary or apprentice employees were shown being subjected to repeated shocks. Investigators found no comparable evidence showing senior employees being seated, questioned and shocked for incorrect answers.

Keller concluded that Tapia, Kayla Gammie, Douglas Boudrias, Christopher Baldwin and Jordon Hutchison violated district rules governing employee conduct and workplace violence.

The report identified Boudrias, Baldwin and Hutchison as leading participants in the conduct and recommended that all three be terminated. Hutchison was also identified as the owner of the device and the person who modified it.

The investigator recommended 48-hour unpaid suspensions for Tapia and Gammie.

Tapia participated in the incidents and recorded the videos, according to the report, but investigators considered his decision to eventually report the behavior and provide evidence to be a mitigating factor.

The report found that Gammie participated in questioning Lohse while he faced being shocked for wrong answers but did not personally operate the device or help construct it. Investigators also noted that she accepted responsibility for her conduct.

The Fire District said it followed the independent investigator's recommendations, terminating three employees and suspending two.

## Earlier report raised concerns about station culture

The newly released documents also include a July 2025 workplace culture analysis of Station 1A conducted by attorney Susan Gainey.

That investigation did not substantiate formal harassment allegations or find specific policy violations. However, more than 30 employees were interviewed, and witnesses described the station as having a culture marked by intense peer pressure, social exclusion, aggressive banter and behavior that sometimes crossed the line between horseplay and hazing.

Some employees reportedly described the station as cliquish and said newer personnel could feel isolated or unwelcome. The report also stated that firefighters had requested transfers, avoided bidding for assignments at the station or considered leaving the district because of the workplace environment.

Gainey recommended reassigning personnel, counseling supervisors and expanding training related to workplace conduct, leadership, conflict de-escalation and professional boundaries.

The Fire District said those personnel reassignments were operational and non-disciplinary because the allegations being examined at the time could not be substantiated through on-the-record testimony.

District administrators said the 2024 videos were concealed from management and did not become known until March 2026, resulting in a separate investigation.

Because some of the employees shown in the videos had previously accused Fire Chief Jeff Lee and District Attorney Kim Sabol of wrongdoing, the district said it hired outside counsel to avoid any appearance that the investigation was retaliatory or biased.

Keller recommended that the matter be reported to law enforcement and the Florida Department of Health in addition to the administrative investigation. The released documents do not state whether criminal charges were filed.

The disciplined employees have initiated the contractual grievance and arbitration process, according to the district. The Fire District said it will present its evidence during that process and does not plan to comment further while it remains pending.

The released materials did not include separate statements from the disciplined employees or their union.

cards.headline: Britain's Josh Kerr breaks 27-year-old mile world record in London
cards.teaser: Josh Kerr ran the mile in 3:42.66 at Saturday's Diamond League event in London, breaking Hicham El Guerrouj's previous mark of 3:43.13 set in 1999.
cards.body:
Kerr made no secret that he was targeting the long-standing record at Saturday's Diamond League event in London. Earlier this week, he revealed he ran 2:42.45 in a 1,200-meter time trial. His sponsor, Brooks, dubbed the effort "Project 222," referencing the number of seconds in 3 minutes, 42 seconds. The shoe company said Friday, "This is the moment Josh Kerr stands to make history and bring the mile record home."

Kerr has emerged as one of the world's top middle-distance runners, winning bronze in the 1,500 meters at the Tokyo Olympics and silver at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Before turning professional, Kerr starred at the University of New Mexico, where he won multiple NCAA titles. He also set an NCAA indoor mile record of 3:35.01 in 2018. Kerr's record-setting run came during the Diamond League, an established international circuit of professional track and field events. American Yared Nuguse finished second in 3:45.69.

cards.headline: Waterspouts spotted over Indian River Lagoon as severe storms batter Sebastian and Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Friday's severe weather left a trail of impacts across the Treasure Coast, including waterspouts over the lagoon, lightning strikes and fires in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
Video sent to the WPTV newsroom from Sebastian showed a large waterspout passing over the Indian River Lagoon Friday afternoon. In Port St. Lucie, WPTV weather spotters captured video of heavy rain moving through the area. Merry Moore O'Rourke said her rain gauge caught over 3 inches. "All of a sudden, it got black. The wind started just raging and the sky had lit up like I have not seen," Moore O'Rourke said. Severe weather stretched all the way to Okeechobee County, where fire rescue crews airlifted a man to the hospital after he was struck by lightning.

Port St. Lucie also saw significant lightning activity. Lucie County Fire District said crews contained a brush fire near the 1900 block of Castinet Lane after reports that a lightning strike ignited vegetation in a nearby lot. At the 900 block of Bellevue Avenue, fire crews responded to an evening house fire. At the time of the storm, WPTV's radar picked up a significant amount of lightning in the area. Lucie County Fire District said it cannot confirm the cause, as the fire marshal's office still needs to investigate. Moore O'Rourke summed up what many across the region felt as the storms moved through. "I mean it was radical. I mean it was it was a little scary," Moore O'Rourke said.

cards.headline: JetBlue cancels Vero Beach to JFK route after nine months, citing low demand
cards.body:
JetBlue is canceling its flight route between Vero Beach Regional Airport and New York's JFK Airport, with the last flights operating on Sept. 9. The airline cited low demand as the reason for ending the route, which launched last December to excitement from Treasure Coast residents hoping for convenient travel options to the Northeast. Brandon Dambeck, interim airport director, said the airline was not seeing the ridership numbers it had hoped for on the JFK route. Dambeck said the decision reflects how the airline industry operates based on demand.

Not everyone agrees the route had a fair shot. Charlie Ahern, who regularly uses JetBlue flights at Vero Beach Regional Airport, said he believes the route would have grown over time. "I think if they hung in there, it would have worked. I think it would have built up pretty good," Ahern said. He praised the convenience of flying out of Vero Beach, saying "It's easy. It's close." The JFK-Vero Beach route was seen as a major win for the Treasure Coast when it launched, providing direct access to one of the nation's busiest airports.

Meanwhile, Dambeck said JetBlue's Boston route is performing well and seeing great demand. Grece Ezzi flew into Vero Beach on JetBlue from Boston on Friday for the first time. The continued success of the Boston service contrasts with the struggles of the JFK route, highlighting how different markets can perform differently even from the same regional airport. Dambeck noted that the door is not closed on the JFK route returning in the future. "They'll evaluate continuously. So just because it's gone now doesn't mean that it never will come back," Dambeck said.

All affected customers will be notified directly by JetBlue and will receive full refunds. JetBlue has not announced whether it plans to add any replacement routes from Vero Beach or if it will adjust frequency on the remaining Boston service. Passengers with upcoming reservations on the discontinued route are encouraged to contact JetBlue directly or check their email for rebooking options and refund information. The cancellation comes after just nine months of service, leaving some travelers disappointed about losing the direct connection to New York.

cards.headline: World Cup Final ticket prices reach $7,700 for cheapest seats, nearly identical to median monthly US household income
cards.teaser: The cheapest ticket on resale sites for Sunday's World Cup Final in New Jersey currently costs about $7,700, nearly identical to what the median U.S. household earns in an entire month.
cards.body:
The cheapest ticket on resale sites currently for sale is about $7,700. That's nearly identical to what the median U.S. household earns in an entire month. If you want to sit in the lower bowl of the stadium, be prepared to spend at least $10,000. The World Cup final is Sunday in New York.

FIFA has faced criticism over the high ticket prices, which it says reflect strong global demand. Tickets for the third-place game in Miami start at about $700. According to Forbes, this year's World Cup Final could end up being the most expensive sports ticket in U.S. history.

cards.headline: Leon County jury orders Florida Rep. Fabian Basabe to pay $450,000 in sexual harassment case
cards.teaser: A Leon County jury found Republican state Rep. Fabian Basabe liable for sexual harassment, battery and defamation, ordering him to pay $450,000 to a former legislative aide, former intern and the aide's mother.
cards.body:
Republican state Rep. Fabian Basabe ended the week facing a $450,000 civil judgment after a Leon County jury found him liable for sexual harassment, battery and defamation. The case was brought by former legislative aide Nicolas Frevola, former intern Jacob Cutbirth and Frevola's mother.

Basabe represented himself despite having no legal training. The trial was repeatedly interrupted by procedural mistakes and violations of the judge's orders. Circuit Judge J. Lee Marsh told him that if an attorney had done half of what he had done, they would have been sanctioned. Basabe told jurors he represented himself because he wanted to demonstrate that he had nothing to hide. After the verdict, however, he acknowledged that proceeding without an attorney was a mistake. Basabe continues to deny the underlying allegations. He has not been criminally charged, and an outside ethics investigation conducted for the Florida House previously reached an inconclusive finding. His political opponents quickly called for his resignation. Basabe is seeking reelection this fall, and the verdict could also renew questions about whether House leaders will pursue disciplinary action.

cards.headline: Florida voter data surfaces in declassified intelligence reports as Trump renews election security push
cards.teaser: Declassified White House records show a Chinese cyber actor downloaded publicly available Florida voter registration information in 2022, though the reports do not indicate ballots or vote totals were altered.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump renewed debate over election security this week with a Thursday address urging Congress to adopt tighter voting restrictions. Declassified intelligence records released by the White House reference Florida among states whose voter information was collected by foreign actors.

One declassified report says a Chinese cyber actor downloaded publicly available Florida voter registration information from commercial websites in 2022. The same actor also obtained records from Colorado, Connecticut, Michigan, Oklahoma and Rhode Island. Another intelligence record lists Florida among 18 states whose voter information was obtained for possible identity matching and public opinion analysis. The 2022 report says the actor's motive was unknown.

The records describe collection of voter information, some of it publicly available, but do not say Florida ballots or vote totals were altered. An earlier federal assessment of the 2022 elections found no evidence that detected foreign cyber activity prevented voting, changed votes or compromised the integrity of ballots. The White House characterized the broader collection effort as a major compromise of American voter data.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff ramps up traffic enforcement with 1,162 stops in four weeks
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is intensifying traffic enforcement this summer, deploying additional deputies to target speeding and reckless driving on Midway Road, U.S. Highway 1 and Indian River Drive.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said traffic is the top concern among residents and described the crackdown as a quality of life issue. Del Toro is using extra deputies from the sheriff's school resource division to boost enforcement while the school year is on break. He is also placing top-performing deputies in areas of concern. Deputies Christopher Rodrigues and Cheyenne Benning are among those targeting high-problem corridors, including Midway Road, U.S. Highway 1 and Indian River Drive. Benning said the county sees a lot of excessive speeding, noting that someone recently passed her on I-95 doing 105 mph. Rodrigues described stopping a driver doing 72 mph on Midway Road and another doing 98 mph on U.S. 1. On Indian River Drive, where the speed limit is 25 mph, his top recorded speed was 73 mph.

In the past four weeks, deputies conducted 1,162 traffic stops, wrote 470 citations and issued 1,728 written warnings. The enforcement push is part of a broader strategy Del Toro put in place when he took office. He eliminated the agency's dedicated traffic unit and made traffic enforcement the responsibility of every deputy. Since 2025, the sheriff's office has issued more than 26,000 citations, a 155% increase.

cards.headline: DEA chief joins Florida fentanyl summit in Orlando as overdose crisis continues
cards.teaser: Teens from anti-drug coalitions across the country joined grieving parents and DEA Administrator Terrance Cole at a Florida summit this week to discuss stopping fentanyl.
cards.body:
The Fentanyl Free America Summit in Orlando drew students from anti-drug coalitions across the country who traveled to learn about the resurgence of fentanyl so they can return home with a message about one of the country's deadliest drug threats. Hannah Kahn, 18, explained that she has a relative who is addicted to methamphetamine, and seeing how that has destroyed his life has encouraged her to prevent that from happening to anybody else. Jasmine Figueroa, 19, advised that drugs are not a taboo topic and that adults should tell young people what cocaine is, noting they're going to get educated one way or another so adults might as well be the first to educate them and tell them the truth about how things are.

This year's summit welcomed the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration as a partner. DEA Administrator Terrance Cole spent time with victim families and discussed the ongoing threat, saying this poison is being manufactured and distributed out of Mexico by the Mexican cartels. Cole pointed to new tools from the current administration, explaining that the president has designated Mexican cartels as foreign terrorists, which opens different avenues for the DEA to target. Mari Rodriguez's daughter, Imam, died of fentanyl poisoning in 2023 after making the mistake of buying a Percocet pill that had fentanyl in it. Rodriguez said the fight against fentanyl should have started in 2009, when the first fentanyl was found on American streets.

hero.headline: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bobby Portis Jr. join Miami Heat in blockbuster trade
hero.teaser: The Miami Heat introduced two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo and forward Bobby Portis Jr. at the Kaseya Center on Thursday, with both players receiving standing ovations from fans.
hero.body:
Thursday afternoon at the Kaseya Center, Heat Head Coach Erik Spoelstra said Pat Riley asked him if he wanted to coach Giannis Antetokounmpo, and he said yes. Antetokounmpo, a two-time MVP, NBA champion and Finals MVP, is coming off back-to-back injury-filled seasons. He said he thrives on pressure and needs it at this point in his career to go to the next level and get out of his comfort zone. The 6'11, 240-pound forward said he feels like whenever he puts his mind to something, he usually accomplishes it, and he feels this is the best route for him to do that. Antetokounmpo said the moment he's coached hard, everyone else is going to follow, and he doesn't want it to be sugar-coated because he needs the truth so he can apply that to the game.

Bobby Portis Jr. said he prides himself on working every day in the summer to get better. He has been coming off the bench his whole career as a sixth man type of guy and said just being aggressive is what he's always been. Portis said he has been playing with Antetokounmpo for six years now, going on seven, and it's been real fun playing with him. He said his relationship with Bam Adebayo has been built off of being competitors. Spoelstra said the squad with Antetokounmpo, Portis and Adebayo will play a lot of positionless ball.

cards.headline: Florida Panthers to open 2026-27 season on road against Stanley Cup Champion Carolina Hurricanes
cards.teaser: The Florida Panthers will begin their 2026-27 NHL regular season with four Western Conference road games before returning to Amerant Bank Arena for their home opener.
cards.body:
The Panthers will open against the 2026 Stanley Cup Champion Carolina Hurricanes on Sept. 29. The road trip continues with a stop in San Jose on Oct. 6. After the four-game road swing, the Panthers will return to South Florida for their home opener on Saturday, Oct. when they welcome the Minnesota Wild to Amerant Bank Arena.

December will feature seven home games, including four special holiday matchups to close out 2026. The Panthers will host the Buffalo Sabres on Dec. Fans will enjoy two consecutive five-game homestands, the first running Dec. 19-30 and the second from March 2-12.

cards.headline: Argentina defeats England 2-1 with late goals, advances to World Cup final Sunday
cards.teaser: Argentina rallied from a 1-0 deficit with goals from Enzo Fernandez and substitute Lautaro Martinez to defeat England in the World Cup semifinal Wednesday.
cards.body:
Trailing 1-0 going into the 85th minute, Argentina rallied for a 2-1 victory over England on Wednesday with goals from Enzo Fernandez and substitute Lautaro Martinez. England's Anthony Gordon scored the opening goal in the 55th minute. Fernandez swept in the equalizer from outside the box in the 85th minute after Messi fed him the ball. Two minutes into stoppage time, Messi sent in a cross for Martinez to head in the winner. Martinez said he told Alexis Mac Allister that he was going to come on and win it. England goalkeeper Jordon Pickford made vital saves while Mac Allister sent a header off the post as Argentina attacks mounted.

The defending champions will take on European champion Spain in the final on Sunday in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said the team proved its collectiveness, brotherhood, and fight to the very end. England lost in the World Cup semifinals for the third time after losses to Germany in 1990 and Croatia in 2018. England also led 1-0 against Italy in the European Championship final in 2021 and lost on penalties. England coach Thomas Tuchel said Argentina played with more risk and rhythm, with the feeling they had nothing to lose anymore, which freed them up and held England back.

cards.headline: Major League Baseball restricts dugout iPad use to prevent artificial intelligence from making game decisions
cards.teaser: MLB made custom tabs on dugout iPads inaccessible to teams starting Wednesday night to prevent the tablets from running artificial intelligence to help make in-game decisions.
cards.body:
Major League Baseball made custom tabs on dugout iPads inaccessible to teams starting Wednesday night, when the second half of the season started, to prevent the tablets from running artificial intelligence to help make decisions. The tablets have access to video and league-provided data, and also included a custom tab where teams could access other programs. MLB executive vice president of baseball operations Morgan Sword wrote in a June 11 memo to general managers, assistant GMs and video coordinators that in many cases, the custom tab had expanded the use of the dugout iPads beyond their originally intended purpose to include recommendations regarding substitutions, pitch calling, and other in-game decisions traditionally made by players and coaches. The memo was first reported by The Athletic and obtained by The Associated Press.

A review by the competition committee found clubs had been compliant with the regulations. Sword wrote that instituting this prohibition beginning with the second half of the season is intended to provide clubs that have relied on the custom tab with appropriate lead-time to make any necessary adjustments. MLB started a pilot program allowing use of iPads in dugouts with restrictions late in the 2015 season and expanded their use in 2016 under a deal with Apple. Video was eliminated in the 2020 COVID season following the Houston Astros' sign-stealing scandal, then returned in 2021.

cards.headline: Flip City Gym and Cheer gymnasts earn top 15 national finish, qualify for Junior Olympics
cards.body:
Three gymnasts from Flip City Gym and Cheer secured a top 15 finish at AAU Nationals in Knoxville, Tennessee last month. Skylar Rose-Daris, Victoria Supan, and Charli Rine competed as a team and came close to a perfect score with a 9.9. Head Coach Candice Lazuka said it's hard to get a perfect 10, but the team got a 9.9 and were very close to a 10. The finish qualified the team for the Junior Olympics in Iowa next month.

The trio competed locally, traveled, and advanced to states and regionals during what Lazuka described as a strong season. Each gymnast found their way to the sport through different paths. Rose-Daris said it wasn't really gymnastics, it was the fact that she knew how to do a cartwheel. Supan was inspired by all the gymnasts that she saw on YouTube, and how amazing they are, and how fun it looks. Rine said she loves it because she learns new things. Looking ahead to the Junior Olympics, Rose-Daris said it's going to be really fun that she's going to an entire different part of the world. Supan described the experience as happy and exciting at the same time. Rine said she is focused on getting first place on floors.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds and David Jolly lead Florida governor's race as primary nears
cards.teaser: Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly hold commanding advantages in their respective primaries as Florida's August 18 gubernatorial primary approaches.
cards.body:
Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds continues to hold a commanding advantage in Republican polling and fundraising, while David Jolly has consolidated support in the Democratic contest. A Tyson Group survey released this week placed Donalds at 48 percent, followed by Lt. Gov. Jay Collins at 9 percent, businessman James Fishback at 8 percent and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 4 percent. About 26 percent of respondents remained undecided. Donalds holds a major financial advantage, with his campaign announcing more than $90 million raised across his campaign operation. President Donald Trump has endorsed Donalds, while Gov. Ron DeSantis has remained publicly neutral in the primary. Collins has not received an endorsement from DeSantis, who appointed him lieutenant governor in August 2025.

Fishback faces a ballot challenge from Collins alleging Fishback lived and voted in Washington, D.C., and does not meet Florida's seven-year residency requirement for governors. A two-day hearing is scheduled to begin July 21 in Tallahassee. Fishback says he was born and raised in Florida, has lived in the state throughout his life and purchased a Washington condo only to visit his parents. On the Democratic side, Jolly moved this week to address his past business and political relationship with Clearwater financier Leo Govoni. Federal prosecutors allege Govoni and accountant John Witeck stole more than $100 million from a nonprofit managing trust funds for people with disabilities.

cards.headline: Democratic Rep. Angie Nixon to stand trial in September on charges from Capitol sit-in
cards.teaser: Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon will stand trial the week of Sept. 21 on misdemeanor charges stemming from her May sit-in outside Gov. Ron DeSantis' Capitol office.
cards.body:
Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon learned she will stand trial the week of Sept. 21 on misdemeanor charges stemming from her May sit-in outside Gov. Ron DeSantis' Capitol office. Nixon and other protesters occupied the area for several hours while objecting to Florida's newly approved congressional map, which could help Republicans add up to four seats in the U.S. Capitol. Capitol Police arrested Nixon after she refused an order to leave.

Nixon calls the prosecution political and has incorporated the case into her campaign for U.S. Senate. Nixon said following Wednesday's hearing that if they think the threat of a trial is going to make her back down, they picked the wrong woman. The trial is scheduled after Florida's Aug. 18 primary, in which Nixon is challenging retired Army Lt. Alex Vindman for the Democratic Senate nomination. Vindman raised $8.5 million during the second quarter and pushed his total receipts above $16 million. Republican Sen. Ashley Moody reported raising another $3.6 million. Moody was appointed to the Senate after Marco Rubio resigned to become secretary of state. The November special election will determine who serves the final two years of Rubio's term.

cards.headline: Orlando fentanyl summit draws teens, grieving parents and DEA chief as overdose crisis continues
cards.teaser: Teens from anti-drug coalitions across the country joined grieving parents and federal law enforcement at the Fentanyl Free America Summit in Orlando this week.
cards.body:
The Fentanyl Free America Summit in Orlando drew students from anti-drug coalitions across the country who traveled to learn about the resurgence of fentanyl so they can return home with a message about one of the country's deadliest drug threats. Hannah Kahn, 18, a summit attendee, said the drug is not widely known because people are not seeking out fentanyl but it is just laced within other drugs. Jasmine Figueroa, 19, said adults should not treat drugs as a taboo topic and should tell young people what cocaine is, noting they will get educated one way or another.

This year's summit welcomed the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration as a partner. DEA Administrator Terrance Cole said the poison is being manufactured and distributed out of Mexico by the Mexican cartels. Cole said the president has designated Mexican cartels as foreign terrorists, which opens different avenues to target them. Mari Rodriguez's daughter, Imam, died of fentanyl poisoning in 2023 after buying a Percocet pill that had fentanyl in it. Rodriguez said the fight against fentanyl in the U.S. should have started in 2009, when the first fentanyl was found on American streets. While deaths from the synthetic opioid are down, tracking how widespread fentanyl has become is nearly impossible in part because of Narcan, an over-the-counter nasal spray that is increasing survival rates.

cards.headline: Security First Insurance lowers Florida homeowners rates by 5.6 percent, launches disappearing deductible
cards.teaser: Security First Insurance is lowering homeowners insurance rates by an average of 5.6 percent, the latest in a series of rate decreases the Florida-based company has made over the last two years.
cards.body:
Security First Insurance is lowering homeowners insurance rates by an average of 5.6%, the latest in a series of rate decreases the Florida-based company has made over the last two years. Melissa Burt DeVriese, president of Security First, said the company is required to pass along all savings to customers, and it has been doing so. Insurance companies have been reducing rates or holding them stable as more companies cite a reduction in lawsuits from state reforms.

Security First also announced new discounts and a disappearing deductible that rewards claims-free customers by reducing their deductible over time. Over the course of five years, the deductible goes down 20 percent each year as long as the customer does not have a loss. Once a loss occurs, the discounted deductible applies, and then it resets back to the full deductible amount. Based in Ormond Beach, Security First has about 155,000 policies in the state and is committed to writing more policies in southeast Florida. Online firm Insurify reports that in 2026 Florida homeowners pay the highest average premium in the country at $8,292. State insurance regulators said that with more companies and more competition, homeowners should seek better premiums by shopping around.

cards.headline: Defense Secretary Hegseth backs low-altitude Blue Angels flyover in Pensacola as safety reviews draw scrutiny
cards.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended low-altitude military flyovers after a Navy Blue Angels jet flew so low over a crowded Pensacola beach Wednesday that chairs and tents went flying, sand kicked up and children held their hands over their ears. The Navy initially said it was conducting a thorough safety review, but Trump administration officials quickly praised the maneuver instead. Hegseth wrote on his personal X account that "the flyovers will continue until morale improves," while Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell posted "Carry on Patriots" alongside a photo showing a Blue Angels jet with a wingtip just feet above beachgoers' heads. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump administration political appointee, said the Navy had no problem with the flight and there would be no reprimands or firings. Navy officials would not say if a routine flight debrief was the thorough safety review the service promised the day before. The White House tweeted a cartoon showing beachgoers photographing a Blue Angels jet with the words "Freedom" and "It's okay to love America."

The incident marks at least the third time Hegseth has voiced support for military maneuvers that drew scrutiny and safety investigations. In March, he ended an Army investigation into helicopters hovering near Kid Rock's Tennessee home, saying "No punishment. Carry on, patriots." Months later, he lifted suspensions of eight South Carolina National Guard helicopter pilots who conducted a low flyover during a July 4 event. In both prior cases, Hegseth's intervention led to the end of safety investigations. Pentagon spokesman Jacob Bliss said he had nothing further to provide when asked if the social media posts meant another investigation had been halted. Aviation safety consultant Jeff Guzzetti, who used to investigate crashes for the National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration, called the behavior reckless and said a cavalier attitude from top military leaders can only lead to accidents. Former Transportation Department Inspector General Mary Schiavo said Blue Angels demonstrations are exceedingly dangerous and not something to be performed over people.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County man leads Martin County deputies on high-speed chase through Indiantown
hero.teaser: A Palm Beach County man led Martin County deputies on a high-speed chase through Indiantown after driving more than 100 mph on State Road 710, forcing other vehicles off the roadway.
hero.body:
Deputies spotted 33-year-old Markell Tillman driving aggressively at speeds exceeding 100 mph on State Road 710, forcing other vehicles off the roadway. When deputies attempted to stop him, Tillman fled. Tillman weaved through traffic in an attempt to lose deputies before turning onto SW Martin Highway toward Palm City, where he continued to drive recklessly.

Deputies spotted Tillman again traveling eastbound on Martin Highway near Allapattah Road. Deputies used stop sticks to disable his vehicle near I-95. Tillman then bailed out of the vehicle and attempted to flee on foot before deputies caught up with him and took him into custody. Tillman was arrested on the following charges: fleeing and eluding, aggravated fleeing with injury or damage, operating a vehicle exceeding the speed limit by 50 or more mph, driving while license suspended or revoked, obstruction without violence, and operating a vehicle at 100 or more mph. Tillman also had an out-of-county warrant at the time of his arrest. He was booked into the Martin County Jail.

cards.headline: Martin County faces $2.1 billion transportation funding gap over next 20 years
cards.teaser: Martin County estimates it will need approximately $2.8 billion for transportation improvements over the next 20 years, but only $701 million is currently available, meaning the county can fund just about one quarter of its identified needs.
cards.body:
The Martin County Metropolitan Planning Organization estimates the county will need approximately $2.8 billion for transportation improvements over the next 20 years. But only $701 million is currently available, meaning the county can fund just about one quarter of its identified needs. Of the $701 million currently available, all but $10 million comes from state and federal funding sources.

Among the most pressing unfunded needs are nine roads the county identified as requiring widening as traffic grows. The total cost to widen those roads is approximately $213 million, money that is not currently available, leaving all nine projects out of the county's draft Cost Feasible Plan. Those roads include SW Martin Downs Boulevard, SR-714/SW Martin Highway, SW 96th Street, SW Bridge Road, CR-714/SW Martin Highway, SW Allapattah Road/CR-609, SE Green River Parkway, SW Indiantown Avenue, and SE Bridge Road/CR-708.

State Road 710 is among the county's highest priorities. The draft plan includes several SR-710 projects that are already funded or programmed, including a realignment at CR-714/Martin Highway, widening from CR-609 to SW Van Buren Road, and additional widening segments totaling nearly 16 miles. Beth Beltran, administrator for Martin County's Metropolitan Planning Organization, said funding shortfalls of this scale are not unusual and that local governments routinely identify transportation needs and then compete for limited state and federal dollars to fund them.

cards.headline: Jonathan Dickinson State Park concession closure leaves visitors without boats and tours
cards.teaser: Jonathan Dickinson State Park's concession operation is closed indefinitely this summer, leaving visitors without access to boat rentals, canoe rentals, and the popular Loxahatchee Queen tour to Trapper Nelson's Island.
cards.body:
Jonathan Dickinson State Park's concession operation is closed indefinitely this summer, leaving visitors without access to boat rentals, canoe rentals, and the popular Loxahatchee Queen tour to Trapper Nelson's Island. Park officials told WPTV the vendor who operated the concession had their contract expire. The park is now searching for a new vendor, but warns the approval process is lengthy and could take months.

Max Santos, a Jupiter local who has been coming to the park his entire life, said he and others were caught off guard when they arrived to find the concession office closed. Santos said the concession had allowed visitors to have access to bike rentals, canoes, motorboats, and even take a tour. After all of those activities, it allowed visitors a place to get refreshments. Daniela Sellitti drove from West Palm Beach with her kids hoping to take them on the Loxahatchee Queen to Trapper Nelson's Island, only to find the service unavailable. Sellitti said it would be nice if the park is able to find a contract with someone else who will come in and open a concession and get the boats running again, so that visitors can enjoy the river and get a chance to go over to Trapper Nelson's, which is a part of Florida history.

cards.headline: Martin County brush fires contained, Florida Forest Service expects more this summer
cards.teaser: Martin County saw two brush fires this week, including one sparked by a lightning strike. Both are now fully contained and being monitored by the Florida Forest Service.
cards.body:
Martin County saw two brush fires this week, including one sparked by a lightning strike. Both are now fully contained and being monitored by the Florida Forest Service. The Florida Forest Service says the conditions that fuel these fires are not going away anytime soon, but residents should not be alarmed.

David Grubitch, a mitigation specialist and spokesperson with the department, said this is their peak season. The summertime heat is drying out fine dead fuels, and when you get a lightning strike, it is going to start a fire, Grubitch said. He explained that rain often extinguishes these fires immediately, but sometimes they travel underground and surface days later. Grubitch said the public plays a crucial role in helping the Florida Forest Service do its job. He stressed that residents should never assume someone else has already called in a brush fire, saying it can make all the difference in how quickly crews are able to get a fire under control.

cards.headline: Safe Kids Treasure Coast providing free pool alarms to Martin County residents
cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Health and Safe Kids Treasure Coast are providing a limited supply of free pool alarms to qualifying residents in Martin County.
cards.body: The Florida Department of Health and Safe Kids Treasure Coast are providing a limited supply of free pool alarms to qualifying residents in Martin County. A pool alarm is one layer of protection and should always be used alongside close adult supervision, pool barriers and water safety education to help prevent drowning, the coalition said. Safe Kids Treasure Coast is asking residents to fill out a survey to determine eligibility. The program is available to Martin County residents with a residential pool, with one alarm per household. There are no income or priority group requirements, and alarms are available while supplies last. A 9-volt battery is required to operate the alarm but is not included, the coalition said. For more information, residents can call (772) 462-3501.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound couple seeks support as husband battles head and neck cancer
cards.teaser: A Hobe Sound couple is asking for community support as they navigate a cancer diagnosis, holding onto faith every step of the way.
cards.body:
Dave and Faren Motz met in South Florida before moving to Maui, where they married and raised their family. Faren raised all three of their kids and home schooled them, and the couple started a business and had a farm where they served children. Years later, they moved to Hobe Sound and purchased a property, but just months after settling in, Dave was diagnosed with head and neck cancer. As the couple searched for healthcare in Florida, AdventHealth in Celebration provided programs and grants that became a critical resource.

Dave underwent nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments. The repeated visits to Orlando, biopsies, scans, and exams added up, costing the couple nearly $20,000 out of pocket. Their age and income kept them from qualifying for Medicare or Medicaid. Doctors told Dave he has an 85% chance of recovery. Dave is a former firefighter who had long been the family's provider, but Faren has stepped up to support them both. Faren works at Latitudes at the Jupiter Beach Resort, where those who want to show their support can stop by and visit. Those who would like to contribute financially can donate to the family's GoFundMe at Standing with Dave Motz in his cancer battle.

cards.headline: Murray Middle School demolition underway after Hurricane Milton tornado damage
cards.body:
Murray Middle School demolition is underway in Martin County, marking the start of a major reconstruction effort following tornado damage caused by Hurricane Milton. The project includes reconstruction of buildings destroyed in the tornadoes, along with a new administration building, media center, art lab, and a full overhaul of the parking lot. The demolition phase alone costs $3.3 million, though the total project cost has not been finalized. The project is being funded by local capital improvement, sales tax and Public Education Capital Outlay. Students who were displaced from the affected classrooms will continue learning in portable classrooms until construction is complete.

Kirstie Gernaine, coordinator of public information and community relations for the Martin County School District, said Murray Middle School was already slated to get all of this construction work with a new admin area, a new media center and a brand new art lab. With Hurricane Milton and those tornadoes destroying the buildings in the back buildings 18, 10, and nine, the district was able to add these on. The school district said parents can be assured their students will be safe during construction. Barriers have already been placed around the work zone to keep students out. The district hopes to complete the renovations by December 2027.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Fire District says 3 fired, 2 suspended after hazing investigation
hero.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District says it terminated three employees and suspended two others following an independent investigation into allegations that senior personnel used a
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District says it terminated three employees and suspended two others following an independent investigation into allegations that senior personnel used a modified bug zapper to electrically shock junior firefighters while they were on duty.

The district released a statement Saturday, July 18, along with a 2025 workplace culture analysis and a May 2026 investigative report detailing the incidents.

According to the documents, firefighter-paramedic Roberto "Rocky" Tapia provided videos and photographs to district administrators in March 2026. Investigators determined that several of the recordings showed incidents that occurred at Station 1 in March and September 2024.

The device was reportedly constructed from a dismantled bug zapper and modified so it could deliver electrical shocks to people.

One video showed then-probationary employee and paramedic apprentice Matthew Lohse seated in a chair while senior employees asked him paramedic-related questions. Investigators said Lohse was shocked when he answered incorrectly as other employees watched and laughed.

Other videos showed then-probationary or apprentice firefighters Kyle Kirkham and John Edmondson being shocked multiple times. The report noted that the employees appeared to experience pain, including yelling, groaning, twitching and pulling away from the device.

Several witnesses told the investigator that the junior employees had consented to participating. Lohse, Kirkham and Edmondson also said they had agreed to be shocked.

However, independent investigator John "J.K." Keller concluded that the power imbalance between senior personnel and probationary employees undermined the credibility of those claims of consent.

The investigation found that only junior, probationary or apprentice employees were shown being subjected to repeated shocks. Investigators found no comparable evidence showing senior employees being seated, questioned and shocked for incorrect answers.

Keller concluded that Tapia, Kayla Gammie, Douglas Boudrias, Christopher Baldwin and Jordon Hutchison violated district rules governing employee conduct and workplace violence.

The report identified Boudrias, Baldwin and Hutchison as leading participants in the conduct and recommended that all three be terminated. Hutchison was also identified as the owner of the device and the person who modified it.

The investigator recommended 48-hour unpaid suspensions for Tapia and Gammie.

Tapia participated in the incidents and recorded the videos, according to the report, but investigators considered his decision to eventually report the behavior and provide evidence to be a mitigating factor.

The report found that Gammie participated in questioning Lohse while he faced being shocked for wrong answers but did not personally operate the device or help construct it. Investigators also noted that she accepted responsibility for her conduct.

The Fire District said it followed the independent investigator's recommendations, terminating three employees and suspending two.

## Earlier report raised concerns about station culture

The newly released documents also include a July 2025 workplace culture analysis of Station 1A conducted by attorney Susan Gainey.

That investigation did not substantiate formal harassment allegations or find specific policy violations. However, more than 30 employees were interviewed, and witnesses described the station as having a culture marked by intense peer pressure, social exclusion, aggressive banter and behavior that sometimes crossed the line between horseplay and hazing.

Some employees reportedly described the station as cliquish and said newer personnel could feel isolated or unwelcome. The report also stated that firefighters had requested transfers, avoided bidding for assignments at the station or considered leaving the district because of the workplace environment.

Gainey recommended reassigning personnel, counseling supervisors and expanding training related to workplace conduct, leadership, conflict de-escalation and professional boundaries.

The Fire District said those personnel reassignments were operational and non-disciplinary because the allegations being examined at the time could not be substantiated through on-the-record testimony.

District administrators said the 2024 videos were concealed from management and did not become known until March 2026, resulting in a separate investigation.

Because some of the employees shown in the videos had previously accused Fire Chief Jeff Lee and District Attorney Kim Sabol of wrongdoing, the district said it hired outside counsel to avoid any appearance that the investigation was retaliatory or biased.

Keller recommended that the matter be reported to law enforcement and the Florida Department of Health in addition to the administrative investigation. The released documents do not state whether criminal charges were filed.

The disciplined employees have initiated the contractual grievance and arbitration process, according to the district. The Fire District said it will present its evidence during that process and does not plan to comment further while it remains pending.

The released materials did not include separate statements from the disciplined employees or their union.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office arrests nephew in fatal shooting of Fort Pierce art teacher Andre Leonard Barnes
cards.teaser: Dale A. Mincey, 41, was formally charged with first-degree murder Saturday in connection with the death of his uncle, 66-year-old Fort Pierce art teacher Andre Leonard Barnes.
cards.body:
Dale A. Mincey, 41, Barnes' nephew, was formally charged with first-degree murder Saturday in connection with Barnes' death. Mincey remains in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail and is being held without bond. The fatal shooting happened July 7 at a residence on the 2700 block of Essex Drive. Deputies responded to the home at around 3:30 p.m. after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned a man had shot another man with a rifle. Barnes was taken to a local hospital, where he died. Deputies said the fatal shooting was premeditated.

Karen Moye, who lived in the home with Mincey and Barnes, was also at the home when the shooting occurred. She heard a loud bang while she was in the bathroom and came out to find Mincey and called police, an arrest affidavit said. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said during a press conference Tuesday that detectives uncovered information indicating Moye, the victim's sister and mother of the suspect, knowingly provided false information to investigators and withheld pertinent information related to the homicide investigation. She has been charged with false report to law enforcement and the commission of a capital felony. Barnes worked as an art teacher for the St. Lucie County School District since 2017, serving at West Gate K-8 and Samuel S. Gaines Academy. He leaves behind three adult children.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff ramps up traffic enforcement with 1,162 stops in four weeks
cards.teaser: Sheriff Richard Del Toro is deploying additional deputies and launching a new targeting initiative aimed at reducing speeding and reckless driving across St. Lucie County this summer.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is intensifying traffic enforcement this summer, deploying additional deputies and launching a new targeting initiative aimed at reducing speeding and reckless driving across the county. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said traffic is the top concern among residents and described the crackdown as a quality of life issue. Del Toro is using extra deputies from the sheriff's school resource division to boost enforcement while the school year is on break. He is also placing top-performing deputies in areas of concern.

Deputies Christopher Rodrigues and Cheyenne Benning are among those targeting high-problem corridors, including Midway Road, U.S. Highway 1 and Indian River Drive. Benning said most recently she had someone pass her on I-95 doing 105 mph. Rodrigues said he stopped a driver doing 72 mph on Midway Road and another doing 98 mph on U.S. Highway 1. On Indian River Drive, where the speed limit is 25 mph, his top stop was 73 mph. In the past four weeks, deputies conducted 1,162 traffic stops, wrote 470 citations and issued 1,728 written warnings. The enforcement push is part of a broader strategy Del Toro put in place when he took office. He eliminated the agency's dedicated traffic unit and made traffic enforcement the responsibility of every deputy. Since 2025, the sheriff's office has issued more than 26,000 citations, a 155% increase.

cards.headline: Villa Del Sol residents return home nearly 2 years after structural damage forced evacuation in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Residents of buildings 3, 4, and 5 at Villa Del Sol in St. Lucie County were notified last month they could return to their condos after an August 2024 inspection found structural damage.
cards.body:
Villa Del Sol residents in St. Lucie County told WPTV they're able to return home after nearly two years of being displaced from their condos. Residents were notified last month they could return after an inspection in August 2024 found structural damage in buildings 3, 4, and 5, which were deemed unsafe. WPTV received emails sent to residents from the Board of Directors telling them they could return. WPTV also obtained a letter from engineers sent to St. Lucie County's Building Department requesting they lift occupancy restrictions following their special inspection. Katie Johnson was the first to share to WPTV that residents had been told they could come back. She described the work still underway at the property, saying they're still moving the dirt back under the buildings.

Robert Segedin took WPTV inside his family's home, excited to return but thinking about those who cannot. Eric Johnson is among those not coming back. He was one of the first residents WPTV met at Villa Del Sol and is now living in Georgia. Eric said the financial toll has been severe, saying they had to drain out all their savings accounts and all their 401ks just trying to make ends meet while this was going on. He is filing for bankruptcy and filing his condo for foreclosure. Katie Johnson said she feels bad that some were hit harder than others with the situation.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce neighbors pack planning meeting over Causeway Cove high-rise development proposal
cards.teaser: The Causeway Cove development project off Seaway Drive includes five high-rise buildings, including a 17-story building standing 192 feet tall, more than four times the city's height limit.
cards.body:
The Causeway Cove development project was reviewed Monday by the Fort Pierce Planning Board. The project, located off Seaway Drive, includes five high-rise buildings, including a 17-story building standing 192 feet tall, more than four times the city's height limit. Plans also call for two hotels and more than 70,000 square feet of retail space. The development qualifies under the Live Local Act, a state law passed in 2023 that allows developers to bypass height and density restrictions as long as they set aside 40% of units for affordable housing for at least 30 years. The project includes more than 900 apartments and condos, with 365 of those designated as affordable housing.

Neighbors packed the chamber Monday as the city's planning board met to review the plans. Buster Brewster, a boater at Causeway Cove Marina, said he worries the project will change the character of the area. Dennis Fein attended the meeting and raised concerns about traffic, saying the city will have massive traffic jams and nobody will be able to get on or off the island. City Planning Director Kev Freeman said developers must add traffic mitigation efforts and any required intersection or access improvements. City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city has been eliminated from the process and does not have a position because this is regulated by the state of Florida in the entirety. City commissioners are scheduled to hear a review of the project as the next step in the process.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie couple fights rezoning of lot behind their home near Tradition
cards.teaser: Joseph and Margaret Mucciolo are searching for answers after Port St. Lucie City Council voted to rezone the lot behind their home from residential to commercial.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie couple is searching for answers after the city council voted to rezone the lot behind their home from residential to commercial, despite their months-long opposition. Margaret Mucciolo said the beautiful setting is what drew them to the property. In a unanimous vote, the Port St. Lucie City Council approved changing the lot behind their yard, where trees currently stand, to be rezoned from residential to commercial. Joseph Mucciolo said in six months or a year, it's going to be gone.

The council says the change is necessary to reduce traffic in the neighborhood. One council member said adding commercial closer to neighborhoods reduces the length of trips, which reduces overall traffic because trips are shorter. The Mucciolos spoke at Monday's meeting, voicing their concerns, but they feel the council left them unheard. The council held its second reading Monday. While there was public comment, it was a quasi-judicial hearing, meaning council members act as a panel of judges, applying existing zoning rules to a specific property and making decisions based strictly on sworn testimony and factual evidence, not public opinion. The Mucciolos say they will be exploring any kind of appeal process to change this outcome or to change the next one.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County woman turns $20 scratch-off into $5 million jackpot
cards.teaser: Maria Duran, 57, claimed a $5 million top prize from the $5,000,000 CROSSWORD CASH scratch-off game on April 6.
cards.body: Florida Lottery officials announced Friday that Maria Duran, 57, claimed a $5 million top prize from the $5,000,000 CROSSWORD CASH scratch-off game on April 6. Duran chose to receive her winnings as a one-time, lump-sum payment of $3,262,138. She purchased her winning ticket from PK 2 Quick Mart, located at 4101 Okeechobee Road in Fort Pierce. The game's overall odds of winning are 1-in-2.90, but the chance of winning $5 million playing this game is 1-in-4,018,135.

hero.headline: Applications open for free or reduced-price school meals in Indian River County
hero.teaser: Families in Indian River County can apply for free or reduced price meals for students starting July 15. Students at six Indian River County schools can receive free meals during the 2026-2027 school year through federal nutrition programs.
hero.body:
Families in Indian River County are able to apply for free or reduced price meals for students starting July 15. Students at six Indian River County schools can receive free meals during the 2026-2027 school year through federal nutrition programs. Other families in the district may still qualify for free or reduced-price meals based on household size and income criteria.

Families are encouraged to complete one application per household to determine eligibility for free or reduced-price school meals. Applicants will need their child's Student ID number, their child's full formal name as listed in FOCUS, a valid email address, and internet access or the LINQ Connect mobile app. Families whose household receives Florida Medicaid benefits should have their 10-digit Medicaid case number that begins with the number 1.

Families can visit www.LINQConnect.com, sign in or create an account, search for Indian River County Public Schools in Vero Beach, add their student using the Student ID and formal name, then start the Meal Application under School Services. Families with questions about the meal programs can contact Shawn O'Keefe, the district's nutrition services director, at 772-564-5041 or shawn.okeefe@indianriverschools.org.
